intro: Punycode converts internationalized domain names (IDNs) between their Unicode form and the ASCII-compatible encoding defined in RFC 3492. Encode mode turns labels containing non-ASCII characters into their xn-- prefixed form, and decode mode reverses any xn-- label back to readable Unicode. It is handy whenever you need to inspect, validate, or troubleshoot how a domain with accented or non-Latin characters is represented on the wire.
useCases: Convert a domain like münchen.de into its xn-- ASCII form for DNS records or registrars
Decode an xn--prefixed hostname seen in logs, certificates, or email headers back to readable Unicode
Inspect IDN homograph or lookalike domains during phishing or security reviews
Verify how a CDN, browser, or DNS provider will store an internationalized domain
Debug URL parsing where a host appears in Punycode but you expect Unicode

faq.q: Is my data sent to a server?
faq.a: No. The conversion runs entirely in your browser using a client-side RFC 3492 implementation, and nothing you type or paste is uploaded anywhere.

faq.q: How does it handle a full domain with multiple labels?
faq.a: The input is split on dots and each label is processed independently. When encoding, only labels containing non-ASCII characters get the xn-- prefix; when decoding, only labels starting with xn-- are converted, and the rest are left unchanged.

faq.q: Why does my decoded label come back in lowercase or unchanged?
faq.a: Decode mode checks for the xn-- prefix case-insensitively, so XN-- works too. Labels without that prefix are passed through as-is, since they are already plain ASCII.

faq.q: What happens with invalid Punycode input?
faq.a: Decoding reports an error for malformed input, such as a non-ASCII character in the basic segment, an invalid digit, an unexpected end of input, or an integer overflow per the RFC 3492 limits.

faq.q: Does it apply IDNA rules like normalization or nameprep?
faq.a: No. This tool performs only the Punycode encode and decode step. It does not run Unicode normalization, case folding, or full IDNA mapping, so prepare your labels accordingly before encoding.
